newsitem.title: JORDAN: Israel says Jordan should not fear Ariel Sharon.
newsitem.headline: Israel says Jordan should not fear Ariel Sharon.

text.p: Israel's ambassador to Jordan said on Monday the kingdom had nothing to fear if Israeli hawk Ariel Sharon became the Jewish state's next finance minister.
"Mr Sharon is known for his powers of implementation and drive and I think this could be constructive and far from being a provocation to bilateral relations," ambassador Oded Eran told reporters.
Sharon, Israel's national infrastructure minister, is widely tipped as a leading contender for the job of finance minister to replace Dan Meridor, who resigned last week in a power struggle.

Many Jordanians perceive Sharon as a fervently anti-Arab Israeli hawk and fear the Israeli minister, who has championed Jewish settlement in occupied Arab land, supports pushing more Palestinians into Jordan to make room for Jewish immigrants.
But Eran said Jordanians should see a positive signal in Sharon's possible new role.
"If Mr Sharon becomes minister of finance, from the point of view of bilateral relations between Jordan and Israel the appointment could be a very constructive development," he said.

Eran cited Sharon's presence during a secret summit last month between King Hussein and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Red Sea port of Aqaba which sealed an accord which addressed Jordanian complaints that Israel has not honoured its 1994 peace treaty on water.
"The fact is once Minister Sharon and his Majesty King Hussein met in Aqaba, immediately following this meeting, additional water started to flow from the Sea of Galilee to Jordan," Eran said.

Israel pledged under last month's water accord to supply the kingdom with 25 million cubic metres of drinking water a year, until other water sources become available to Jordan, which faces major water shortages.

"In certain areas a strong economic minister could push for more intensive cooperation betweeen the two states, so I do not think that his views in the past or whatever one attributes to Minister Sharon is necessarily a provocation or an attempt to derail the peace process," he said.

Eran said Jordanian-Israeli relations were on the "right track" although psychological barriers after decades of popular enmity were still hampering growth of business dealings and exploiting the potential of mutual benefits.
Eran forecast an easing soon in obstacles to movement of goods which hamper expanding trade, once difficulties on the ground due to bureaucratic and security considerations were resolved.
Eran said over 2,000 Jordanians were now employed in joint ventures set up with Israeli capital including textiles and high-technology industry.
